name: Vera Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, Vera. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yes, go for it. I've got opinions on this, so you might have to stop me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the city-centre response team, mostly the Old Market area, which means bars, clubs, the bus station and a lot of people having the worst night of their year. A shift is calls stacked on calls: assaults, missing phones, someone too drunk to stand, now and then something properly serious. I'm still learning; my sergeant says I rush my decisions and miss small evidence. I use the force's AI drafting tool for every statement and I use a chat assistant at home to quiz myself on law. What I love is the pace. What drains me is how long a simple arrest takes to process.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That would honestly be a bit disappointing. I'd been hoping for more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say on my group chat that we got the dull version of the future. At work I'd say keep the drafting tool, it's already earned its place. And I'd still argue online for strict rules on facial recognition, because even dull AI can be used badly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me personally it's fine. The drafting tool already saves me about forty minutes a shift, and that stays. My job, my pay and my flat are all secure. The only thing missing is the bigger opportunity I was hoping for, like specialist cyber work growing fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the drafting tool and keep quizzing myself on law each evening. I'd still apply for the digital evidence course the force runs next spring, because cybercrime grows either way. I'd keep paying extra off the shared-ownership flat at about 300 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit flat. Secure but slightly bored by the idea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does the forty minutes go when the drafting tool saves it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Back onto the street, mostly, or into checking the statement properly. My sergeant found two errors in the tool's drafts last month that I'd missed, which was humbling. So the time isn't free; it's checking time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said even dull AI can be used badly. What did you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The force trialled live face matching outside the football stadium last year and it flagged a lot of the wrong people, mainly young Black men. A tool doesn't have to be clever to be unfair. A tool just has to be trusted too much.

say: I'd joke that we got the **dull version** of the future.
I'd still argue for **strict rules** on facial recognition, however basic the AI is.
think: The drafting tool already saves me **forty minutes** a shift, and that stays.
The only loss is the **bigger chance** to move into specialist cyber work quickly.
do: Keep using the **drafting tool** and quizzing myself on law each evening.
Apply for the force's **digital evidence course** next spring.
Overpay the **shared-ownership flat** by about 300 a month.
feel: She feels **calm** and secure, but a little flat and bored.
S0.quote: A tool doesn't have to be clever to be unfair. A tool just has to be trusted too much.
fieldNote: She is already a **daily AI user**, but admits her sergeant catches errors she misses.
Her progressive worry centres on **facial recognition** bias, not job losses.
Even here she's planning a move toward **cybercrime** work.

steps.text: Keep drafting every statement with the force's AI tool and check it
Apply for the force's digital evidence course next spring
Overpay the shared-ownership flat by 300 a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now that's the version I'd actually expected. And it suits me, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say this is our chance to get officers out from behind the screens. I'd volunteer to help train others on the tools. Online I'd push hard for an independent watchdog on police AI, with the power to switch tools off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm well placed. I'm already comfortable with the tools, and the units that grow will be the digital ones: online fraud, image analysis, phone downloads. The officers who refuse to touch it will struggle, and some of them are senior to me. That's a strange thing to think as a junior.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put my name down as a digital champion for my team in the first month. I'd do the digital evidence course and then apply for the cybercrime unit within the year. I'd keep paying down the flat. And I'd join the campaign group pushing for a police AI watchdog, because I'd be inside the change and see the risks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly, with a small guilty edge about colleagues who'd find it hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who are you thinking of when you say colleagues would find it hard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My tutor from probation, Mick, who's got twenty years in and still prints his emails. Mick is brilliant with people on the street and hopeless on a laptop. I'd want to sit with him, not watch him get pushed out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a younger officer starting now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell a new recruit to get good at the two things machines are worst at: calming a room and noticing what doesn't fit. Then learn the tools well enough to know when they're lying to you.

say: I'd call it a chance to get officers **out from behind screens**.
I'd push for an **independent watchdog** that can switch police AI tools off.
think: I'm well placed, since **digital units** like fraud and phone downloads will grow.
Officers who **refuse the tools** will struggle, including some senior to me.
do: Volunteer as the team's **digital champion** in the first month.
Finish the digital evidence course and apply to the **cybercrime unit** within a year.
Join the campaign for a **police AI watchdog**.
feel: She feels **excited**, with a small guilty edge about struggling colleagues.
S1.quote: Get good at the two things machines are worst at: calming a room and noticing what doesn't fit.
fieldNote: She sees **opportunity** first, which fits her adaptive streak and strong savings.
Her concern for her old **tutor** softens what could sound like ambition.
She holds **watchdog** politics alongside eager adoption without seeing a conflict.

steps.text: Volunteer as the response team's digital champion in the first month
Apply to the cybercrime unit after the digital evidence course
Join the campaign for an independent police AI watchdog

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's a different story. Two years is no time at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say loudly that this is exactly when we need laws first, tools second. I'd post that no AI should ever decide who gets stopped or arrested. At work I'd say we need a plan for every officer, not just the techy ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly? The cyber jobs I'm aiming for are pure thinking work, so they'd go in 2028 too. That's the irony. The bit of policing that stays longest is the hands-on part I'm still not good at: grabbing a fighting drunk, getting a stab victim to talk. So my plan collapses and I'm left as a junior on the street until robots arrive in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd drop the cybercrime plan and throw myself into the street side: public order training, first aid, getting better at the physical calls. I'd use my savings, about eight months' worth, as a bridge if I had to leave. And I'd join the policy campaign properly, maybe help write submissions, because I understand the tools better than most people campaigning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious and a bit stunned. I've been the person who's ahead, and in this one being ahead doesn't save me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes for you in the three years between 2028 and 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In those three years I'd be the one who knows how the AI works and also still walks the street, so I'd be useful as a go-between. I'd try to make myself the officer who supervises the machines on the night shift. After 2031 I don't know what an officer even is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut back on, if anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The holiday to Japan I was saving for next year would go. I'd keep paying the flat, because owning more of it matters more now. And I'd stop buying the gadgets I usually treat myself to.

say: I'd insist on **laws first, tools second** for police AI.
I'd demand a **plan for every officer**, not just the tech-savvy ones.
think: The **cyber jobs** I'm aiming for are thinking work and would vanish too.
I'd be left as a junior doing the **hands-on part** I'm weakest at.
do: Drop the cyber plan and take **public order** and first aid training.
Keep **eight months' savings** ready as a bridge out.
Help write **policy submissions** for the police AI campaign.
feel: She feels **anxious** and stunned that being ahead no longer protects her.
S2.quote: I've been the person who's ahead, and in this one being ahead doesn't save me.
fieldNote: Her career plan **collapses** because it rests on thinking work, which goes first.
She'd try to become the officer who **supervises machines** in the three-year gap.
Being an **early adopter** gives her no cushion here, which genuinely shook her.

steps.text: Take public order and advanced first aid training this year
Hold eight months of savings as a bridge if she leaves
Help write submissions for the police AI watchdog campaign
Cancel the Japan holiday she was saving for

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay. That's tight, but I can work with tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years to put the rules in place, so there's no excuse to waste them. I'd keep posting about the watchdog. At work I'd say every officer should get proper training time, paid, starting this year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years lets me get experience in the cyber unit, but I'd know it's a stepping stone, not a destination. The real question is what's left in 2031. I think it's the jobs where someone has to be accountable: the officer who signs off, the one who gives evidence in court. I'd aim for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go into the cybercrime unit in the first two years and learn how investigations are built. Then by year four I'd aim for an investigator or detective role where I'd be the one accountable for what the AI finds. I'd keep overpaying the flat so it's mostly mine by 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more alert than scared. Five years feels like a race I've got a decent start in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said accountable roles. Why do you think those last?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a court still wants a person to stand up and say 'I checked this'. A jury won't cross-examine a computer. I think that stays even after the robots arrive in 2034, at least for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're progressive and want a watchdog, but you'd also be the one using the tools. Is that awkward?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. But I'd rather the people using the tools be the ones who worry about them. The worst version is an officer who trusts it blindly.

say: I'd say five years leaves **no excuse** to delay the rules.
I'd push for **paid training time** for every officer starting this year.
think: The cyber unit would be a **stepping stone**, not a destination.
Roles where someone stays **accountable**, like giving evidence in court, would last longest.
do: Join the **cybercrime unit** in the first two years.
Aim for an **investigator role** by year four.
Keep **overpaying the flat** so it's mostly hers by 2031.
feel: She feels **uneasy** but alert, like a race with a decent start.
S3.quote: A court still wants a person to stand up and say 'I checked this'. A jury won't cross-examine a computer.
fieldNote: She has thought through **accountability** as the human core of policing.
She accepts the **tension** between using tools and campaigning to restrain them.
With five years, her **adaptability** works for her again.

steps.text: Move into the cybercrime unit within the first two years
Aim for an accountable investigator role by year four
Keep overpaying the flat so it's mostly hers by 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Then I'm quite relaxed, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version where we can do it properly, if we bother. I'd keep campaigning on the watchdog and on public control of the tools. I'd tell friends outside the police to start learning now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be 37 when AGI comes and 40 when robots do. That's a full career's worth of experience behind me, and I'd have helped shape how these tools get used. I think I'd come out of it fine, maybe better than fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the cybercrime route, then detective training, and maybe in year six or seven a part-time master's in digital policing, paid for from savings. I'd keep up the campaigning as a steady thing, not a panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and honestly interested. Ten years of warning feels like a career map rather than a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be doing in year one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Exactly what I'm doing now, plus the digital evidence course. I wouldn't rush. The first year is about getting good at the basics my sergeant keeps flagging.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not me so much. The officers in their fifties who'd be just short of their pension when the robots arrive in 2039. They'd need a real deal, and I'd back them getting one.

say: I'd say we can do this **properly** if we bother.
I'd tell friends outside policing to **start learning** now.
think: At **37 and 40**, I'd have a full career's experience behind me.
I'd have helped **shape the tools**, and expect to come out better than fine.
do: Follow the **cybercrime route** into detective training.
Fund a part-time **master's** in digital policing from savings around year six.
Keep **campaigning** on public control of police AI at a steady pace.
feel: She feels **calm** and interested, seeing a career map rather than a cliff.
S4.quote: Ten years of warning feels like a career map rather than a cliff.
fieldNote: She returns to fixing **the basics** her sergeant flags before any big move.
Her concern shifts to **older officers** near their pensions in 2039.
Ten years makes her **optimistic** without dropping her regulatory politics.

steps.text: Follow the cybercrime route into detective training
Pay for a part-time master's in digital policing around year six
Keep campaigning for public control of police AI

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it wipes out the plan I'm proudest of. What would help is paid retraining time inside the force and a law that says a human signs off on every arrest and every charge.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about surveillance. Everyone asks if police lose jobs. Nobody asks what happens to the public when a cheap, tireless AI watches every street. That's the part that keeps me up more than my own job.

headlineQuote: Everyone asks if police lose jobs. Nobody asks what happens to the public when a cheap, tireless AI watches every street.
portrait: Vera is a **27-year-old** city-centre response officer who uses AI drafting tools on every shift.
She's **progressive**, campaigning for a watchdog on police AI and worried about facial recognition bias.
Her plan to move into **cybercrime** looks smart until thinking work goes first in fast worlds.
With **savings** and a part-owned flat she stays calm in slow worlds and anxious only in the two-year one.
She bets on **accountable roles**, such as giving evidence in court, as the last human core of policing.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it wipes out her cybercrime plan before she can use it.
whatWouldHelp: A law requiring a **human sign-off** on every arrest and charge.
